name: Helicopters
description: Rotor craft that hover, climb and fly on a gyroscopic rotor.

pages.title: Helicopters
pages.text:
[#](FFFFFF)[#]() **Key points**

- Lift from a **Gyroscopic Propeller Bearing** facing up on a mast above the cabin.
- The rotor sits **over the centre of mass**.
- A **Wooden Propeller on a Swivel Bearing** at the tail pushes and steers.
- Needs **brass** for the bearing's Gyroscopic Mechanism.

pages.title: Staying upright
pages.text: A Gyroscopic Propeller Bearing keeps its push pointing straight up, up to 12 degrees off its own axis, whatever the cabin does.

With the rotor well above the weight, the cabin hangs under it like a pendulum and rights itself: kicked to 14 degrees, a test craft rocked back level. A plain Propeller Bearing pushes the way the cabin points, and the same kick rolled it over.

pages.title: Over the weight
pages.text: The bearing can lean its push only 12 degrees, so the rotor must sit over the centre of mass. On a compact craft the rotor stands only a few blocks above the weight, and one block of engines or tail along the keel tips it several degrees: balance it with the tail's length, not by leaning the rotor.

pages.title: Sizing the rotor
pages.text: A rotor pushes 0.2 x sails^1.5 x RPM and draws 2 stress units per sail per RPM, so on the same engines a bigger, slower rotor lifts more. A rotor of 56 sails, 15 blocks across, at a Portable Engine's own 32 RPM pushes about 2700 and draws 3584 stress units. Its push thins with the air, which sets the ceiling.

pages.title: Which way it pushes
pages.text: The bearing's value panel (or a wrench) sets which way it pushes for the way it turns: "Push air when clockwise" or "Pull air when clockwise". Set it so the rotor lifts: on the other setting it presses the craft into the ground. Rotors here don't twist the cabin, so a helicopter needs no tail rotor against that.

pages.title: Up and down
pages.text: The collective is an Analog Transmission in the rotor's line on a Throttle Lever: forward climbs, back sinks, and in between it hovers. Near the ground it hovers about halfway back; high up, where the air is thin, only a notch or two back. A two-seater climbs about 4 blocks a second low down.

pages.title: Going places
pages.text: The rotor stays level, so tipping the cabin doesn't drive it along. A Wooden Propeller at the tail, geared up to 256 RPM and pushing level with the centre of mass, drives it forward on its own Throttle Lever; the test two-seater flew about 8 blocks a second.

pages.title: Steering
pages.text: The tail propeller hangs under a Swivel Bearing that the Steering Wheel swings. Nothing grips the air sideways, so it yaws on the spot: an upright fin of several Symmetric Sails at the tail damps that.

With a 2 by 3 fin it turned about 23 degrees a second at full wheel and stopped a second or two after the wheel came back; with one of 2 sails it kept spinning up and coasted half a turn. After a turn it slides on the way it was going for a few seconds and loses speed, so steer early.

pages.title: Keep the disc clear
pages.text: Nothing may stand in the plane the blades sweep or touch them from above or below: the blades strike it, and a fin touching a blade tip was enough for the tail to break off the moment the rotor spun up. Hang fins under the boom or keep them a block below the blades.

pages.title: Glue and assembly
pages.text: Glue the gearbox and propeller under the Swivel Bearing in their own small Super Glue box, apart from the rest: glued in with the ship, they stay behind when the swivel takes its propeller.
Assemble with the Physics Assembler while every engine is off, then right-click the Swivel Bearing with an empty hand; light the engines last, or the rotor loses its blades.

pages.title: A helicopter that flies
pages.text: A two-seater, 15 x 9 x 19: a closed 7 by 7 cabin on log skids, four Portable Engines in its back row, a 56-sail rotor 15 blocks across at 32 RPM, a tail boom to a swivelled Wooden Propeller at 256 RPM and a fin under it.
It lifts off level, climbs about 4 blocks a second, tops out near y 205 and turns about 23 degrees a second (flown in a test world).

pages.title: Ask the Book
pages.text: Where the book has its voice, ask it for a helicopter (one to three seats) and it lays one out, sized, balanced and checked, as a 3D model you can save as a schematic.
